findings.issue_text: packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleEmailReminders.ts:44 — P2, confidence 100, advisory wrong-shape/cascading-failure: `const remindersToCancel = await prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({` materializes the entire due cancellation queue and `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` awaits one SendGrid request per row before reaching the independent scheduling query at line 80, so a cancellation burst with aggregate provider latency greater than an unscheduled reminder’s remaining lead time delays unrelated users’ reminders past their send time; the strongest rebuttal is that the one-hour predicate bounds work, but it bounds dates rather than row count, and the deletion test is to remove cancellation draining from this scheduling handler and process bounded batches independently.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx:576 — P2, confidence 100, advisory soft-delete/performance: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId);` now retains scheduled email rows with `cancelled: true` while the query at lines 507–510 still loads every generation using `workflowStepId: oldStep.id`, so an organizer repeatedly editing a workflow before its reminders enter the one-hour cancellation window accumulates and rewrites all prior cancelled generations, producing quadratic cancellation updates across edits and increasing database load; the strongest rebuttal is that the cron eventually deletes these rows, but rows scheduled up to 72 hours ahead remain throughout those edits, and the deletion test is to exclude already-cancelled rows from active-reminder reads so their repeated update branches disappear.

packages/features/ee/workflows/lib/reminders/emailReminderManager.ts:200 — P3, confidence 100, advisory coupling/simplification: `immediateDelete?: boolean` gives the same deletion API three incompatible ownership rules—delete the database row when there is no reference, cancel only the provider when true, or retain a pending database cancellation otherwise—forcing seven lifecycle call sites to repeat provider dispatch and understand persistence policy, with the two rescheduling entry points already choosing different guarantees at handleNewBooking.ts:968 and bookings.tsx:490; the strongest rebuttal is that parent deletion requires immediate cancellation, but a positional boolean exposes that storage constraint without expressing who completes cleanup, and the deletion test is to centralize provider dispatch and use explicit cancellation operations with documented persistence postconditions, removing the seven repeated EMAIL/SMS branch pairs and the boolean mode.

packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts:484 — P2, confidence 100, advisory: `//Workflows - cancel all reminders for cancelled bookings` excludes paid bookings because `if (bookingToDelete && bookingToDelete.paid)` returns `return { message: "Booking successfully cancelled." };` at line 464 before either reminder manager executes, leaving paid customers receiving reminders after a successful refund and cancellation; the strongest rebuttal is that this bypass predates the patch, but it defeats the stated comprehensive booking-lifecycle coverage and needs an explicit exclusion or inclusion in the acceptance criteria.

packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleEmailReminders.ts:48 — P2, confidence 100, advisory: `lte: dayjs().add(1, "hour").toISOString()` introduces a time-sensitive cancellation boundary without behavioral verification of a cancelled reminder at 61, 60, and 59 minutes before delivery or a cron invocation crossing its delivery time, leaving reviewers unable to establish the required no-reminder-after-cancellation guarantee from the supplied static-only evidence; the strongest rebuttal is that existing scheduling behavior already uses an hourly boundary, but the patch newly makes cancellation depend on that boundary and needs a fake-clock lifecycle test plus a provider cancellation-contract check rather than inference from scheduling behavior.

packages/prisma/migrations/20230217230604_add_cancelled_to_workflow_reminder/migration.sql:2 — P1, confidence 75: Editing the existing migration to add `ALTER TABLE "WorkflowReminder" ADD COLUMN     "cancelled" BOOLEAN;` leaves databases that already applied the empty HEAD~2 migration without this column because Prisma does not reapply recorded migrations, so the new `cancelled: true` query and reminder updates fail after upgrade; add a new migration instead.

packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleEmailReminders.ts:57 — [P2, confidence 100] When one cancellation request rejects, `await client.request({` exits the entire loop before `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete);`, so every subsequent reminder is skipped and the lazy Prisma deletes already collected for successful cancellations never execute, leaving unrelated cancelled bookings scheduled at SendGrid for this run.

packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts:488 — P1, confidence 100: the unawaited `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId);` replaces the previously awaited reminder deletion, so a failed cancellation-marker update is swallowed by the manager and the handler returns `Booking successfully cancelled.` while the reminder remains active and invisible to the cancellation cron; the same loss of awaited persistence occurs when disabling workflows and requesting reschedules.

packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleEmailReminders.ts:57 — P1, confidence 100: a single rejected `await client.request({` exits the cancellation loop into its outer catch, skips every remaining reminder and the deferred `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete);`, and still returns HTTP 200, so one bad batch prevents otherwise valid cancellations and even successful earlier cancellations retain their database rows for replay.

packages/features/ee/workflows/lib/reminders/emailReminderManager.ts:213 — P1, confidence 100: the `if (immediateDelete) {` branch never persists `cancelled: true` and its request failures are swallowed, so a transient SendGrid failure during the newly added direct-reschedule cancellation leaves the old email scheduled permanently outside the cron's `cancelled: true` retry selection while the reschedule proceeds successfully.

packages/features/ee/workflows/api/scheduleEmailReminders.ts:56 — P1, confidence 75, advisory: `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel) {` serially awaits outbound cancellation calls with no configured timeout or query limit before scheduling any email, so a stalled provider call or a cancellation backlog exceeding the request lifetime prevents pending emails from being scheduled; the strongest rebuttal is that hosting timeouts bound execution, but terminating the request abandons the untouched scheduling work instead of bounding and progressing each batch.

goldens.comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new code at lines 44-80 in scheduleEmailReminders.ts processes cancellations sequentially (for...of with await) before handling unscheduled reminders. This is a valid architectural concern - if there are many cancelled reminders, the sequential SendGrid API calls could delay the scheduling of new reminders. However, this is not a bug per se - the code will still function correctly, just potentially with delays. The one-hour time window does provide some bound, but the concern about row count vs time bound is valid. This is a legitimate performance/architecture concern introduced by the diff, making it an important non-bug issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx:576 — P2, confidence 100, advisory soft-delete/performance: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId);` now retains scheduled email rows with `cancelled: true` while the query at lines 507–510 still loads every generation using `workflowStepId: oldStep.id`, so an organizer repeatedly editing a workflow before its reminders enter the one-hour cancellation window accumulates and rewrites all prior cancelled generations, producing quadratic cancellation updates across edits and increasing database load; the strongest rebuttal is that the cron eventually deletes these rows, but rows scheduled up to 72 hours ahead remain throughout those edits, and the deletion test is to exclude already-cancelled rows from active-reminder reads so their repeated update branches disappear.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real performance concern in the diff. Looking at the code: when `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called without `immediateDelete=true` (line 576), it sets `cancelled: true` on the reminder row rather than deleting it. Meanwhile, the query at lines 507-510 in workflows.tsx fetches reminders using `workflowStepId: oldStep.id` without filtering out cancelled reminders. This means if a user edits a workflow multiple times before the cron job runs (which processes reminders scheduled within 1 hour), each edit will re-fetch and re-update all previously cancelled reminders. This is a valid architectural/performance concern introduced by the soft-delete pattern, though it's not a correctness bug - the system will still function correctly, just with unnecessary database operations.
